docs.title: Export a training set
docs.text:
skytwin-export renders frames of a scene and writes them with YOLO or COCO labels, ready for Ultralytics, DETR or another detector. This page exports 20 frames of an example scene, cut into 640 px tiles, in both formats.

Before you start, you need:

  • Python 3.10 or later and a Rust toolchain, to build the skytwin package.
  • A checkout of this repository, for examples/dirty-frame.json.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install the package from the repository root:
pip install ./crates/skytwin-py
  1. Export the frames:
skytwin-export examples/dirty-frame.json out/ --frames 20 --format yolo --format coco --tile 640 --overlap 64

Frame k is the scene's frame k with seed + k, so running the command again with a larger --frames extends the same set.

  1. Point your trainer at the output. For Ultralytics, give it out/data.yaml; for COCO tools, out/annotations/instances_train.json and instances_val.json.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The scene's 1024 × 1024 frames each give four tiles. The last 10% of the frames form the validation split, so out/images/train/ holds 72 PNG tiles and out/images/val/ holds 8, each with a label file in out/labels/. Stars are class 0 and satellites class 1.

The labels reference lists every option, the output files and the label formats.

docs.title: Load frames in PyTorch
docs.text:
To train without writing files, skytwin.torch renders frames on the fly. It needs PyTorch installed. count sets how many frames the dataset holds; without it, the scene's batch.frames or 1:

from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from skytwin.torch import FrameDataset, collate, detection_target

dataset = FrameDataset("examples/dirty-frame.json", count=1000, transform=detection_target)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=16, num_workers=4, collate_fn=collate)
for images, targets in loader:
    targets[0]["boxes"], targets[0]["labels"]

Frames hold different numbers of objects, so collate stacks the images and keeps the targets as a list, one per frame.

docs.title: Training labels reference
docs.text: The label record in the truth file, the classes and boxes built from it, and the files skytwin-export writes for YOLO (Ultralytics) and COCO tools such as DETR. Export a training set gives the steps; design/labels.md explains how the signal-to-noise ratio is computed and why the rules below were chosen.

docs.title: Labels in the truth file
docs.text:
Each star, streak and target in the truth file has a label that records what a detector could see of it.

Field Meaning path Pixel positions along which the source was drawn, pointing motion included. A still source has one point. A moving one has the path from its first to its last lit point, simplified to within 0.5 px and to at most 65 points, with both ends kept. Empty when nothing was drawn. snr Signal-to-noise ratio of an ideal matched filter, √(Σ sᵢ² / vᵢ) over the source's pixels on the image, where sᵢ is its expected signal in electrons after the flat field and vᵢ the pixel's variance. No detector can do better. peak_snr Highest single-pixel signal-to-noise ratio, max sᵢ / √vᵢ. extent_px Distance from path of the farthest pixel centre where the source is at least the pixel's noise σ, in pixels. saturated Whether a pixel where the source is at least the noise σ saturates, counting everything on that pixel: it reaches full well, or the level where the delivered pixel clips at the output's maximum, whichever is lower.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: skytwin.labels.objects reads the labels of a frame. Stars are class star. Targets and pixel streaks are class satellite. A source is a streak when the farthest two points of its path are more than twice the camera FWHM apart, and otherwise a point. With by_form, each class splits into star_point, star_streak, satellite_point and satellite_streak.

docs.title: Boxes
docs.text:
The labelled region of an object is its path widened by a radius. The radius is extent_px or the FWHM, whichever is larger, plus 0.5 px to reach the edges of the outermost pixels. An object is labelled when its snr is at least min_snr, 5 by default.

Skytwin puts pixel centres on whole numbers, while YOLO and COCO measure from the outer corner of the first pixel. Labels therefore add 0.5 px to each axis. x runs along a row of the image array and y down its rows. Images are written with array row 0 at the top, so a FITS viewer that draws row 0 at the bottom shows the same frame flipped vertically.

docs.title: Tiles
docs.text: A large frame can be cut into tiles. A point is kept in a tile when at least half of its box lies inside. A streak is kept when part of its path lies inside. Its signal-to-noise ratio in the tile is its full value times the square root of the share of its on-image length inside. Axis-aligned boxes are clamped to the tile. A streak's rotated box runs along its part in the tile from the first to the last point, with the half-width of its radius. Where it crosses the edge of the tile, the edge cuts it, so the box holds all of the streak's light inside the tile; a cut box has four corners but is no longer a rectangle (YOLO-OBB and COCO's rotated_box give the corners).

docs.title: Export options
docs.text:
skytwin-export SCENE OUT_DIR takes these options:

Option Effect Default --frames Frames to render the scene's batch.frames, else 1 --start First frame index 0 --seed Replaces the scene's seed the scene's --format yolo, yolo-obb or coco; repeat for several. yolo and yolo-obb both write labels/, so choose one. yolo --classes Kinds to label, separated by commas: star, satellite, or star,satellite star,satellite --by-form Split each kind into point and streak classes off --min-snr Least matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio in the tile 5 --min-visible Least share of a point's box inside a tile 0.5 --min-radius Least box half-width before the half pixel, px FWHM --streak-px Least span of a streak's path, px 2 × FWHM --tile, --overlap Tile size and least overlap, px; the overlap is at least 0 and below the tile size whole frame, 0 --val Share of frames for validation 0.1 --image asinh (8-bit) or raw16 (the delivered pixels in 16 bits) asinh --workers Render threads every core --keep-truth Also write each frame's truth file to truth/ off --overwrite Replace an earlier export in the output folder; without it, a folder that holds one is refused off

Frame k is the scene's frame k, with seed + k, so a set can be rebuilt or extended exactly. The last --val share of the frames forms the validation split, and all tiles of a frame stay in its split.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
The output folder holds:

images/{train,val}/000123.png              000123_04.png for tile 4
labels/{train,val}/000123.txt              YOLO or YOLO-OBB
data.yaml                                  Ultralytics dataset file
annotations/instances_{train,val}.json     COCO
skytwin.json                               scene, options and counts

YOLO label lines are class cx cy w h, and YOLO-OBB lines are class x1 y1 x2 y2 x3 y3 x4 y4, all as fractions of the tile size. COCO category ids start at 1, image file names are relative to images/<split>/, and each annotation carries a skytwin record with the form, signal-to-noise ratio, saturation, rotated box and the source's place in the truth file. COCOeval keeps 100 detections per image by default, and a tile of stars can hold more. Raise params.maxDets when stars are a class.

docs.title: Image stretch
docs.text:
The asinh image measures each pixel in units of the frame's noise, z = (image − median) / σ, with σ = 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation. z is clipped to [−2, 1000] and mapped through asinh(z / 3) linearly onto 0–255. The sky sits at grey level 22, ±1σ of noise spans 11 to 34, a 5σ pixel is at 68, and a 50σ pixel at 148.

The raw16 image keeps the delivered pixel values, so most of a frame sits in a narrow band near its sky level. A reader that converts 16-bit PNG files to 8 bits on loading, as OpenCV's cv2.imread does by default, leaves the sky in a few grey levels and faint sources gone; give such a reader asinh images, or load raw16 files with cv2.IMREAD_UNCHANGED.

docs.title: PyTorch
docs.text: skytwin.torch.detection_target turns a frame into the stretched image, scaled to 0–1, and a target with boxes (xyxy in pixels, as torchvision detectors take, or cxcywh as fractions, as DETR takes), labels and snr. Frames hold different numbers of objects, so batch them with skytwin.torch.collate.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Hot pixels and radiation hits are in the truth file (instrument.hot_pixels, instrument.radiation.hits) but are not exported as classes.
  • Labels give boxes and paths. There are no per-pixel masks.
  • The footprint leaves out smear and bleeding along columns. saturated marks the sources that bleed.

docs.title: Learn a profile from real frames
docs.text:
skytwin-calibrate learn turns a folder of an instrument's FITS frames into an instrument profile, with a report of where each setting came from and how closely simulated frames match the real ones.

Before you start, you need:

  • Python 3.10 or later and a Rust toolchain.
  • A checkout of this repository.
  • Sample FITS frames from one camera, as a folder, files, glob patterns or a .txt list.
  • Optional: a star catalogue covering the frames' fields, either a Gaia CSV with Skytwin's column names or a UCAC4 directory. Without one, the zeropoint, colour term and real-sky twins are not learned. design/calibration.md says which to choose.
  • Optional: Fayde (pip install fayde) and a UCAC4 directory (--ucac4), to plate solve frames that carry no celestial WCS of their own. A Gaia CSV alone isn't enough for the plate solves.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Build skytwin and install the tool from the repository root:
cargo build --release
pip install -e tools/calibrate
  1. Learn the profile:
skytwin-calibrate learn FRAMES_DIR -o profile.json --skytwin target/release/skytwin --catalog GAIA_CSV

Leave out --skytwin to skip the refinement and the realism report, and --catalog to skip the steps that need stars.

  1. Open profile.learn.md. Each setting is marked measured, header, default or not learned, with its evidence, and the realism report follows.

  2. If the report shows a header card read wrongly, such as the exposure time taken from the wrong keyword, correct it in profile.keywords.json and learn again with --keywords profile.keywords.json.

  3. Print the profile's summary and a scene to start from:

skytwin-calibrate describe profile.json

docs.title: Result
docs.text: profile.json is ready for a scene's instrument. Blocks that learn does not fit, such as pointing motion and CTI, are listed in the report; add them by hand from the profile reference. Use and override an instrument profile shows how a scene uses it.

docs.title: Add calibration frames
docs.text: Give the camera's bias, dark and flat frames with --calibration DIR. Gain, read noise, dark current, cosmic rays and dust shadows then come from them instead of the science frames.

docs.title: Learn from ground frames
docs.text: Frames with an airmass or altitude in their headers are treated as taken from the ground, and the profile's zeropoint is the one above the atmosphere. When the frames span too little airmass to fit the extinction, give it with --extinction (mag/airmass); the report marks it as assumed. Give the scene's ground site the extinction that the profile's description names.

docs.title: Give spacecraft states
docs.text: When the headers carry no spacecraft position, give --ephemeris a CSV or a JPL Horizons vector table; the command-line reference gives the format. Each frame gets the state at its time and, when its headers give none, its sub-satellite point. Radiation maps and twins matched in orbit need it.

docs.title: Run the steps one at a time
docs.text:
The commands learn runs can also be run separately, for example to build on a base profile whose smear, stray light, layout or header blocks you measured by hand.

  1. Write a keyword map for your instrument's headers, starting from examples/keywords.json.

  2. Measure the archive:

skytwin-calibrate measure --list frames.txt --keywords keywords.json -o real.json
  1. Fit the PSF from frames where stars are points, and put the result in the base profile's camera.fwhm_px and psf.wings:
skytwin-calibrate psf --list point_frames.txt -o psf.json
  1. Build the profile on top of the base profile:
skytwin-calibrate profile real.json --base base.json -o profile.json
  1. Refine it in place (simulate, measure, correct; two passes by default):
skytwin-calibrate refine profile.json --real real.json --keywords keywords.json --skytwin target/release/skytwin
  1. Simulate twins of real frames and compare them:
skytwin-calibrate twins profile.json --real real.json --keywords keywords.json --skytwin target/release/skytwin --ucac4 /path/to/ucac4 -o sim.json
skytwin-calibrate report --real real.json --sim sim.json -o report.md

docs.title: Score a detector
docs.text:
Render a frame, run a detector on it, and score its source list against the truth:

skytwin scene.json frame.fits
fayde detect --image frame.fits -o frame.sources.fits
skytwin-calibrate score --truth frame.truth.json --sources frame.sources.fits -o score.json

score.json holds completeness by magnitude, false detections, and centroid error in units of each star's Cramér–Rao bound; design/calibration.md explains that bound.

docs.title: Use and override an instrument profile
docs.text:
A scene renders through an instrument profile and can change any of the profile's settings without editing the profile file. In this guide, you render a frame through the example profile with its radiation switched off and its dark current drawn anew for each frame.

Before you start, you need:

  • The skytwin command (see the README).
  • A checkout of this repository, for profiles/example-microsat.json.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Create quiet-frame.json and name the profile with instrument:
{
  "seed": 3,
  "instrument": "profiles/example-microsat.json",
  "scene": {
    "random_stars": { "count": 300, "max_flux_e": 500000.0, "min_flux_e": 300.0 }
  }
}

Without an instrument, the scene renders through a defect-free default camera.

  1. Add an overrides object to change settings. It is a JSON merge patch (RFC 7386): objects merge key by key, and any other value replaces the profile's.
"overrides": { "camera": { "exposure_s": 3.0 } }

A top-level camera object in the scene is merged into the profile's camera the same way.

  1. Switch a defect off by setting its block to null, which deletes it from the profile:
"overrides": { "camera": { "exposure_s": 3.0 }, "radiation": null }
  1. To vary a setting from frame to frame, give a distribution where the profile has a number. The example profile fixes its dark current at 0.3 e⁻/s at −30 °C. To draw it for each frame instead, add this dark entry inside overrides, after "radiation": null:
"dark": { "e_per_s_at_ref": { "uniform": [0.1, 0.5] } }

The profile reference lists every distribution and how to link settings so they are drawn together.

  1. Render the frame from the repository root:
skytwin quiet-frame.json out/quiet-frame.fits

docs.title: Result
docs.text: out/quiet-frame.fits has no radiation hits. out/quiet-frame.truth.json records the profile name and, under instrument.settings, every value drawn for the frame. Here, radiation_rate_per_cm2_s is 0, and dark_e_per_s is the dark current drawn from 0.1 to 0.5 e⁻/s and scaled to the frame's temperature.

docs.title: Use a learned profile with its catalogue
docs.text:
A learned profile names the star catalogue it was calibrated against, so the scene gives only the catalogue file:

  1. Print the profile's summary and a scene to start from:
skytwin-calibrate describe profiles/wise-w1.json
  1. Check that your copy of the catalogue matches the profile's (columns, rows, SHA-256):
skytwin-calibrate check profiles/wise-w1.json --catalog /data/gaia_dr3_g17.csv
  1. Give the file in the scene: "catalog": {"path": "/data/gaia_dr3_g17.csv"}. Skytwin fills in the kind, columns, epoch and magnitude limit from the profile.

profiles/README.md lists the learned profiles and what each needs, such as a ground site's extinction.
