docs.title: Scene, truth and header reference
docs.text: What a scene file may hold, what the truth file records, and the FITS keywords Skytwin writes. Instrument profiles are described in reference/profile.md.

docs.title: Scene file
docs.text:
A scene file is a JSON object. All its keys are optional: seed, instrument (a profile path or object), camera and overrides (merged into the profile), scene, and either batch or sequence.

batch makes independent frames for a training set. frames is the number of frames. Frame k uses seed + k and draws everything random anew: stars, streaks, noise, and every profile distribution. With random_pointing, each frame also gets a new pointing. Right ascension and roll are uniform, and declination is uniform on the sphere within dec_deg (default [-90, 90]).

sequence (frames, cadence_s start to start, and a scene.time) makes several frames in a row: frame k starts k × cadence later with seed + k, writes name_000.fits, name_001.fits, …, and the run writes name.sequence.json listing them. Detector maps (hot and flickering pixels, column offsets) stay the same in every frame. With "only_visible": "<target>", frames are kept only when that target is sunlit and not blocked by the Earth; the run steps on at the cadence (up to max_steps, default 100 × frames) and the index records how many steps were skipped. Two settings make the pointing change slowly through a sequence (they need scene.pointing as RA/Dec): pointing_walk (step_arcsec per axis and roll_step_deg, σ per frame) moves the boresight and the header with it; settling (offset_arcsec, time_s) starts the boresight off the commanded pointing, in a direction drawn once, and converges on it as exp(−t / time_s), while the header reports the commanded pointing, so the header lags. The index lists each frame's walk and settling offsets. See the files in examples/. Unknown keys are errors.

  • Pixel positions are 0-based, with pixel centres on whole numbers.
  • Sky positions are ICRS degrees and need scene.pointing.
  • scene.catalog reads ucac4 (a UCAC4 directory) or csv: a local catalogue file such as a Gaia archive extract, with path, columns (default Gaia DR3 names: source_id, ra, dec, phot_g_mean_mag, pmra, pmdec, parallax, bp_rp) and epoch_jyear (default 2016.0). Stars move by proper motion to the observation epoch, carry their parallax, and use bp_rp as the colour index. With an instrument profile that names its catalogue, {"path": "..."} is enough: the profile supplies the kind, columns, epoch and magnitude limit (see reference/profile.md).
  • Roll is the position angle of the image +y axis, east of north, as in Fayde.
  • Brightness is flux_e (total electrons over the exposure) or mag (in the camera band, through camera.zeropoint_mag, the magnitude giving 1 e⁻/s).
  • scene.stars lists stars. Each has a pixel position (x, y) or a sky position (ra_deg, dec_deg), a brightness, and optionally id, color_index, teff_k, and parallax_mas. parallax_mas applies only to a sky position in a scene with a time.
  • scene.random_stars (count, min_flux_e, max_flux_e) adds count stars placed uniformly over the image, with fluxes between min_flux_e and max_flux_e that follow N(>F) ∝ F^−0.6.
  • scene.streaks lists streaks in pixels. Each has a start and an end ([x, y] at shutter open and at shutter close) and a brightness.
  • scene.time.start_utc is the shutter-open time. With a time, catalogue stars move to mid-exposure and aberration is applied.
  • scene.observer is "geocenter" (default), {"tle": [line1, line2]}, {"state_vector": {...}} or {"ephemeris": [...]}, all in GCRS km and km/s, or a ground site: {"site": {"latitude_deg", "longitude_deg", "height_m", "dut1_s", "refraction", "pressure_hpa", "temperature_c", "extinction_mag_per_airmass"}} (WGS84, turning with the Earth at UT1 = UTC + dut1_s; pressure and temperature default to the standard atmosphere at the site's height). A ground site needs a pointing: every source is refracted towards the zenith and dimmed by the extinction at the boresight's airmass, and what is below the horizon is hidden. See examples/ground-tracks-meo.json.
  • scene.pointing.quaternion is [w, x, y, z], rotating camera vectors into GCRS. The camera frame has +z along the boresight, +x along increasing columns and +y along decreasing rows.
  • scene.pointing.track names a target to follow, with roll_deg.
  • scene.targets lists targets: name, orbit (same forms as the observer) and brightness: {"mag": m} (when fully sunlit), {"lambertian_sphere": {"diameter_m": d, "albedo": a}}, or {"facets": {...}}: flat panels, each with a body-frame normal, area_m2, diffuse_albedo, specular_albedo and specular_exponent, in an inertial attitude (quaternion) or tumbling about an axis at rate_deg_s. Panels glint when their normal bisects the Sun and the observer; the path tracer starts fine enough to catch the shortest glint. See examples/tumbling-glint.json. Set "earthshine": true or "moonshine": true on a target to add sunlight reflected by the Earth (Bond albedo 0.306) or the Moon (0.11), each treated as a sunlit Lambertian sphere seen from the target (a far-field approximation, rough within a few Earth radii). The truth records the share that is direct sunlight. scene.target_file reads a two- or three-line element file, with one brightness model for all of it.
  • camera.sun_mag (default −26.74, V) sets the Sun's magnitude in the camera band, or camera.passband computes it, with an AB zeropoint, from a throughput curve and aperture (see reference/profile.md).
  • camera.earth_limb_margin_km (default 100) is the height below which a line of sight counts as blocked.
  • scene.random_streaks (count, length_px, mag, each a fixed value or a distribution) adds straight streaks anywhere on the image in random directions, drawn anew each frame, for training sets.
  • scene.header_bias_arcsec ([east, north]) is the reported pointing minus the true pointing, as from a header that lags the boresight. It adds to the profile's random header error.

docs.title: Truth file
docs.text:
Each star records photons (reaching the detector, before camera.quantum_efficiency and the flat) and detected_e (electrons expected after the flat, averaged over the pixels the star's light falls on); each target records photons too.

For each star in a static frame (no tracking, no pointing motion), the truth file gives the Cramér–Rao bound on its centroid (crlb_px) and flux (crlb_flux_e): the best precision any method could reach, from the actual PSF and noise at that spot. tools/calibrate's score command uses it to grade detectors.

When stars trail (tracking a target, or pointing drift, wobble and jumps), each star also gives trail_start and trail_end: its pixel position at shutter open and close. With x, y (the mid-exposure position) they let a solver's along-trail and cross-trail errors be measured directly.

Pixel positions in the truth are where each source was drawn. Pointing motion is measured from the image at mid-exposure, so it leaves x, y in place and moves the trail ends, a streak's start and end, and a target's start and end samples. A streak's start_radec and end_radec are sky positions, which pointing motion does not change.

For each target, start, mid and end give the pixel position, the astrometric RA/Dec (light-time corrected; what a reduction against the stars reports, consistent with the header WCS), range, phase angle, lit fraction, whether the Earth blocks it, and magnitude. flux_e is the signal drawn and on_image says whether any lit part of the path falls on the image, and light_curve gives the signal rate along the traced path.

Every star, streak and target also has a label for detector training: the path along which it was drawn, its matched-filter and peak signal-to-noise ratios against the frame's noise, how far from the path it stands above the noise, and whether it saturates. See labels.md.

docs.title: Header keywords
docs.text: Keyword Meaning DATE-OBS, DATE-BEG, DATE-AVG, DATE-END, MJD-OBS, MJD-AVG Exposure times, UTC OBS_X … OBS_VZ Observer GCRS position (km) and velocity (km/s) at mid-exposure SITELAT, SITELONG, SITEELEV, AIRMASS Ground site (WGS84 degrees, metres) and airmass at the boresight ATT_RA, ATT_DEC, ATT_ROLL, ATT_QW … ATT_QZ Apparent boresight and camera quaternion CRVAL, CRPIX, CD TAN WCS to astrometric (catalogue) positions; TAN-SIP with A/B/AP/BP terms when the camera has distortion

docs.title: Checks against independent tools
docs.text:
• A frame rendered from UCAC4 is plate-solved by Fayde to 0.01″ of the true centre; one from a 790 km orbit to 0.044″ of the header WCS.
  • A GEO satellite seen from LEO matches an independent Python calculation to 0.024″, 0.0 m in range and 0.0001 mag.
  • Time scales and orbits are checked against astropy and the Python sgp4 package.
  • For each profile learned from a real archive, How close they are in profiles/README.md gives the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance between the statistics of its real frames and those of their simulated twins.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
The same scene file and seed give the same pixels on every machine; continuous integration renders reference scenes on Linux, macOS and Windows and compares the pixel hashes. Frames of a batch run on all cores, and the output doesn't depend on the thread count.

Each pixel's noise comes from its own random stream, so adding or moving a source changes no pixel outside its footprint: the same seed with and without a satellite gives an exact clean/dirty pair. Every run writes name.provenance.json with the Skytwin version, command, seed, status, and SHA-256 hashes of the scene, profile, catalogue and every output.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: On a 16-core Apple M4 Max, a 1024 × 1024 frame through the example profile renders at about 43 frames a second.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: Skytwin follows semantic versioning. While the version is 0.x, a breaking change increases the minor number, and anything else increases the patch number.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
The following changes are breaking:

  • Removing a command-line option or a Python argument, or changing its meaning
  • Removing or renaming a key of a scene file or an instrument profile, or changing what an existing key means
  • Removing or renaming a field of the truth file, the provenance record or an exported label set
  • Changing the pixels a scene and seed give, outside a documented fix
  • Changing a published package's public API so that existing code no longer works

Adding a truth field or an optional scene or profile key whose default keeps old files rendering the same isn't a breaking change. A fix that changes pixels is listed in the changelog with the scenes it affects.

A fix that leaves outputs and file formats unchanged is a patch release. So is a new command, option or truth field that changes nothing that already exists.

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text:
Before Skytwin removes or renames a command-line option, a Python argument, or a scene, profile or truth key, one release deprecates it:

  1. The release that deprecates it still accepts the old name and behaves as before. Skytwin prints a warning that names the replacement, and the release notes list the deprecation.
  2. A later breaking release removes it, no earlier than the next minor version.

A change that can't keep the old behavior can't be deprecated first. Its release notes say what to do, for example to update your scene files.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text: Each release has a section in the changelog that lists its changes and marks the breaking ones. Each release publishes the same version on GitHub, on PyPI as the skytwin package, and on crates.io as the skytwin-core and skytwin-cli crates. You install skytwin-calibrate from the repository; it carries the same version.

docs.title: How skytwin-calibrate learns a profile
docs.text:
Every number comes from measuring frames: real frames to set the profile, and simulated frames, measured with the same code, to check and correct it. Nothing about a particular instrument is built in. Its header names go in a keyword map; its measured profile stays with you.

The steps for running it are in learn-a-profile.md, its commands in the calibrate reference, and every option in the command-line reference.

docs.title: The learn pipeline
docs.text:
learn runs these steps in order:

  1. Headers: finds exposure, time, temperature (°C or K), sub-satellite point, Earth-limb angle, spacecraft position and velocity (and their frame, preferring the exposure start), pointing, roll, tracking rate, gain, read noise, binning, pixel size and pixel scale, by scoring every card on its name and its comment. The pixel size is taken as after binning (as XPIXSZ is) unless its comment says otherwise.
  2. Frames: keeps the most common size and binning; other modes are listed, to learn separately.
  3. Camera: gain, read noise, pixel scale and exposure from headers; leading columns that get no light; pixel type; the saturation level (where frame maxima pile up). Then the read-out chain: a serial lag (noise correlated along rows as aᵏ, sources trailing one way: noise.serial_lag), and, when the headers give no gain, gain and read noise by photon transfer from pairs of frames with the same exposure, taken up to 1.5 times the archive's usual spacing apart (5 to 60 s): the clipped block variance of the difference against level, over the central half of the frame, with the lag's variance reduction undone. On frames with the bias still in, the read noise comes from the darkest frames.
  4. Statistics: background, noise, ramps, pattern noise and sharp events per frame (measure). On frames whose bias sits below the clip, noise comes from quantiles above the clip, where the MAD would read 0. Rows the read-out corrupted (salt-and-pepper bands, dropped rows) are counted and kept out of the sharp events; each row's spread comes from neighbouring-pixel differences, so glare gradients and dense radiation storms are not mistaken for corruption. The odd/even row offset (even rows' level minus their odd neighbours') is measured per frame. The corrupted bands found (rows, and whether noise, dropped or saturated) become readout_faults.
  5. Detector: hot pixels from the median, over 150 frames, of each pixel's excess over its neighbours, and how their rates follow temperature, from the longest exposures that number at least 10 frames (a row's dark charge while it waits to be read does not scale with the exposure, so short frames would inflate the rates); the flat field (a circular field stop if there is one, vignetting inside it, and pixel response non-uniformity) from how each pixel follows the frame level; the PSF from frames whose stars measure round (with any serial lag undone first), picked from all the inputs by their header tracking rate; frame-transfer smear from the column excess above and below bright unsaturated stars (corrected against simulated frames with --skytwin).
  6. Pointing: when the frames carry their own celestial WCS (an archive's Astrometry.net solutions, say), at least 20 of them do, and --skytwin and a catalogue (--catalog or --ucac4) are given, stars are matched to the catalogue through it, and a joint fit over up to 80 frames (per frame an affine map of tangent-plane coordinates, shared radial distortion about the image centre) gives the pixel scale, parity, camera.distortion (kept when k1 is 5σ from zero) and the photometric zeropoint. This works where a fresh plate solve fails (fields tens of degrees wide, a few dozen bright stars). Otherwise, with --ucac4 (a CSV catalogue is not enough) and Fayde (pip install fayde): plate solves of the frames with round stars give the true pixel scale and parity, the roll keyword's convention, the pixel the header RA/Dec refers to, the header's pointing errors, and the photometric zeropoint (aperture photometry of the matched catalogue stars, corrected to total flux with the fitted PSF).
  7. Earth glare, with --skytwin: a tiny twin of each frame gives Skytwin's own geometry (angle from the limb, sunlit or dark limb, Earth's direction in the image); the background of sunlit-limb frames against angle gives the table, dark-limb frames the dark factor, and the frame ramps the gradient and its direction. Frames inside the glare zone leave the pedestal sampling so their glare is not counted twice. Then noise.smooth_field: smooth background structure with sources masked, from block-to-block covariances that hold no pixel noise. With --skytwin it is corrected against simulated frames, twins of the real sky when a catalogue and the frames' pointing are known (frames with their own WCS give it), since a real field's faint stars below the mask add to the covariance too.
  8. Header style, so simulated frames carry the same keywords: constant cards copied, computable ones templated.
  9. Profile blocks from the statistics (profile).
  10. With --skytwin: two refinement passes, then simulated twins and a realism report. Add --catalog or --ucac4 for twins of the real sky.

docs.title: Blocks fitted indirectly
docs.text: skytwin-calibrate learn fits most blocks, the read-out faults among them, directly from frame statistics. The blocks below are fitted indirectly.

docs.title: Background light, pedestal and fixed field
docs.text: skytwin-calibrate learn splits each frame's level into sky_e_per_s, the pedestal and noise.fixed_field when the flat has a field stop: block medians are fitted as pedestal + fixed field + light × flat, the fixed field kept orthogonal to a constant and to the flat's shape.

docs.title: Serial lag
docs.text: skytwin-calibrate learn takes a as the ratio of the lag-2 to the lag-1 correlation of the background along rows (white noise added after the filter lowers both alike), the side from where resolved stars carry more flux, and undoes the lag before choosing frames and fitting the PSF, so the PSF is the optical one.

docs.title: Smooth background field
docs.text: skytwin-calibrate learn measures noise.smooth_field with sources masked: block medians about a quadratic surface, whose covariances between neighbouring blocks (lags 1 and 2) hold no pixel noise. Their ratio gives the scale and their size the RMS, through a table made by measuring simulated fields the same way.

docs.title: Colour term
docs.text: skytwin-calibrate learn fits camera.color_term from forced photometry when its catalogue carries a colour (a Gaia CSV): per-star zeropoint against colour, clipped, kept when 5σ from zero.

docs.title: Choosing a catalogue
docs.text: The catalogue sets the photometry, so use one whose magnitudes hold for the stars the camera sees: UCAC4's own magnitudes saturate brighter than about 8, which a wide-field camera's stars often are. The zeropoint comes from forced photometry at every catalogue position (no detection bias), and learn warns when it drifts with magnitude. With a colour column (bp_rp) it also fits camera.color_term. Gaia DR3 lacks many stars brighter than G ~ 3, often the brightest in a wide field; add_bright_stars.py adds them to a Gaia CSV from the Yale Bright Star Catalogue (VizieR V/50).

docs.title: Calibration frames
docs.text:
With --calibration, learn also reads the camera's bias, dark and flat frames. They are sorted by their header frame type (IMAGETYP and kin), else by the folder or file name, and only those of the science frames' size and binning are used. What they measure replaces what the science frames would give:

  • gain by photon transfer from pairs of flats at the same exposure, with the read noise from pairs of bias frames;
  • the dark current from master darks of the longest and shortest exposure, so the bias and the charge a row collects while it waits to be read cancel (the part that does not grow with exposure is reported, not kept);
  • the radiation rate from hits in the darks, each dark less the median of its night and exposure, leaving out hits at pixels that fire in two or more darks (flickering pixels); with two or more exposures, the hits at zero exposure give the read-out time;
  • dust shadows from the master flat, found with ring-shaped matched filters and measured from their radial profiles, in chip pixels as Skytwin draws them.

Hot pixels stay the ones the science frames show; the darks' own are the fallback when the science frames find none, and profile.learn.md compares the two.

docs.title: Frames whose stars trail
docs.text:
When the stars in most sampled frames trail (a telescope tracking a satellite, say), learn measures each frame's trail length and angle from the frame's autocorrelation, which for segments of length L is a ridge whose profile along the trail is a triangle of half-width L. Then:

  • the PSF comes from the profile across isolated trails, which the motion does not blur; for a sum of round Gaussians the profile across is the same sum of one-dimensional Gaussians, so the fit gives camera.fwhm_px and psf.wings directly;
  • frames with their own WCS are matched by trail centres, found with a filter along the trail, and the zeropoint comes from boxes along the trails, corrected for the PSF halo outside the box and in its background ring;
  • radiation is counted outside the trails in frames of the longest exposure, leaving out events at a pixel that fires in two or more frames (hot and flickering pixels, a tracked target); the read-out time comes from how the hits split between the chip's halves, and the rate is an upper bound, since every other event counts too;
  • each frame's twin trails at that frame's rate, so the smooth-field correction and the realism report compare like with like.

docs.title: Ground frames
docs.text: Frames with an airmass, or the telescope's altitude, in their headers are taken from the ground. Their zeropoint is fitted against airmass, frame by frame, so the profile's zeropoint is the one above the atmosphere and its description gives the extinction a scene's ground site should use (a site applies the atmosphere itself). When the frames span too little airmass to fit it, --extinction (mag/airmass, 0.2 if not given) moves the zeropoint up from the frames' median airmass, and the report says it was assumed. Forced photometry uses an aperture of 2.5 times the PSF's FWHM, with the background 1.36 to 2 apertures out, so a wide PSF's wings do not land in the background. With plate solves, a --catalog (a Gaia extract, say) is measured through each solution, so the colour term and the extinction come from it rather than from UCAC4's magnitudes.

docs.title: The Cramér–Rao bound in scores
docs.text: Truth files of static frames (no tracking, no pointing motion) carry each star's Cramér–Rao bound (crlb_px, crlb_flux_e), from the actual PSF and per-pixel variance. A detector whose centroid errors have an RMS of 1 in units of the bound reaches the best precision any method can.

docs.title: How training labels are computed
docs.text: The labels reference lists the fields and rules. This page explains how the signal-to-noise ratio is computed and why the classes, tiles and image stretch work as they do.

docs.title: Signal-to-noise ratio
docs.text:
While the renderer draws a source, it keeps the electrons the source adds near its path. The reach covers every PSF component that carries at least 5% of the light, out to 5σ + 2 px, grown by the field PSF at the farthest corner of the image. After the sky, the other sources, the flat field, smear, dark current and hot pixels are in place, the renderer weighs each source against the variance of the pixels under it. That variance is the expected signal plus read noise and extra white noise, the same as for the Cramér–Rao bounds. Radiation hits, pattern noise and read-out faults are not part of it.

The signal-to-noise ratio is the expected value for the frame, computed from the noise-free image. Through the example profile it agrees to 0.01% with the value computed from the difference of two noise-free frames rendered with and without the source.

docs.title: Point or streak
docs.text:
A source is a streak when the farthest two points of its path are more than twice the camera FWHM apart. The span, rather than the path length, keeps pointing jitter and small jumps from turning a point into a streak.

In a frame that tracks a target at its rate, every star trails into a star_streak and the target stays a satellite_point. In a frame that stares at the stars, satellites that cross the field are satellite_streak. examples/track-rate.json tracks a GEO satellite from a 790 km orbit through the example profile. In 3 s its stars trail about 45 px.

docs.title: Signal-to-noise ratio in a tile
docs.text: A streak cut by a tile edge keeps its full signal-to-noise ratio times the square root of the share of its on-image length inside the tile, since the squared matched-filter ratio adds over pixels.

docs.title: Image stretch
docs.text: The asinh stretch measures each pixel in units of the frame's own noise before mapping it to grey levels. The grey level of a pixel then depends on its signal-to-noise ratio alone, in every frame and through every profile.

docs.title: Checked with
docs.text: Ultralytics 8.4 reads both YOLO layouts with no corrupt labels and trains on them, and pycocotools reads the COCO files.

docs.title: Realism of simulated frames
docs.text: Simulated frames are usually far cleaner than real ones. Detectors and solvers tuned on clean frames then fail on real data. Skytwin's aim is to reproduce a real instrument's defects closely enough that a detector cannot tell the difference by its statistics.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Every defect is a setting. Nothing about an instrument is hard-coded. An instrument profile (a JSON file, one per satellite or camera) holds every setting. A scene names a profile and may override any field.
  2. Every defect can be switched off. Leaving a block out of a profile turns that defect off, so each one can be studied alone.
  3. Settings vary from frame to frame. Any defect setting in a profile can be fixed or drawn per frame from a distribution, so a simulated set spreads the way a real archive does.
  4. Profiles are measured, not guessed. A calibration step measures a real archive (pedestal, noise, pattern noise, hit rates by orbit position, hot pixels by temperature, gradients by Earth-limb angle, and more) and writes the profile.
  5. Realism is checked. The same measurements run on simulated frames, and a report compares the two distributions; profiles/README.md gives the comparison for each shipped profile.

The repository ships a generic example profile and profiles learned from public archives (a space-based near-infrared imager, WISE's 3.4 µm band and two ground telescopes); profiles/README.md lists them with their sources. A profile learned from your own instrument's frames stays with you.

The keys are in the instrument profile reference, and calibration.md describes how skytwin-calibrate learns them.

docs.title: Moving PSFs
docs.text: A field-dependent PSF is an elliptical Gaussian. It stays closed-form when moving, because in coordinates whitened by its covariance it is a round Gaussian moving in a straight line. A real PSF's halo is usually fitted well by two or three Gaussians out to a few core widths. Fit the components with pixel integration included: fitting point-sampled Gaussians to a stacked star profile counts the pixel width twice and gives too wide a core.

docs.title: Passband colours
docs.text: camera.passband treats every source as a blackbody. Blackbodies miss absorption bands, so colour offsets for cool stars are rough (a few tenths of a magnitude across wide bands).

docs.title: skytwin-calibrate reference
docs.text: Every command, the files learn writes, and what it leaves out. learn-a-profile.md gives the steps; design/calibration.md explains how each block is measured.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Does learn Learns a whole profile from sample frames in one step: the commands below, in order, with header and catalogue handling around them check Compares a local star catalogue with the one a profile was calibrated against: columns, rows and SHA-256 describe Prints what a profile is, what it needs, and a scene to start from measure Per frame: background level, noise (MAD, or quantiles above the clip on mostly clipped frames), clipped fraction, ramps along x and y, residual structure, the strongest coherent pattern (period, angle, amplitude), sharp single-pixel events, corrupted read-out rows, the odd/even row offset, saturated pixels, and header values through the keyword map psf Stacks isolated, unsaturated stars and fits a core plus two wider Gaussians by forward modelling (pixel-integrated stars at random sub-pixel positions, stacked with the same code) profile Sets pedestal, extra white noise, pattern amplitude and read-out ramps as rows linked per real frame; pattern period and angle; temperature; a radiation rate map by sub-satellite point, and the frame-to-frame spread around it (radiation.map_scale, with the Poisson scatter of the counts taken out) refine Scales the pattern amplitude by real/simulated medians; corrects the radiation map cell by cell from twins matched in time, position, exposure and temperature twins Simulates frames that take only time, spacecraft state, exposure and temperature from real frames; everything else is drawn from the profile. With --ucac4 and a pointing in the keyword map, twins show the real sky: catalogue stars at the real pointing, trailed at the recorded tracking rate (trail_rate_arcsec_per_s). Without it they use random stars, which saturate more than a real field report Real and simulated distributions side by side, with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance per quantity score Matches a detector's source list (FITS table with X, Y, such as Fayde's; or CSV/JSON with x, y) to a truth file: completeness by magnitude, false detections (those on streaks, targets, hot or flickering pixels and radiation hits are counted apart), centroid error and bias, and error over each star's Cramér–Rao bound

docs.title: learn options
docs.text: skytwin-calibrate learn INPUTS -o profile.json takes frames as directories, files, glob patterns or .txt lists. skytwin-calibrate learn --help lists every option with its default, and the command-line reference shows the same.

docs.title: Files learn writes
docs.text:
File Holds profile.json The instrument profile, ready for skytwin profile.learn.md Every setting with where it came from (measured, header, default, not learned) and the evidence, then the realism report profile.keywords.json The header keyword map it worked out; edit and pass back with --keywords if a choice is wrong

The profile carries its contract: schema_version, sensor, learned (provenance) and catalog, the catalogue it was calibrated against; a CSV is pinned by SHA-256 and row count. The profile reference lists the keys.

docs.title: What learn leaves out
docs.text:
These are not learned, so they are left out of the profile and listed in the report: Sun and Moon glare, pointing motion (wobble, drift, jumps), CTI, flickering pixels and the field-dependent PSF. Add them by hand from the profile reference.

Some settings need the data to vary. The flat field needs frame levels spanning at least 30 ADU; the temperature trend needs at least 3 °C. With too little variation, learn says so and leaves the block out.

profile keeps the blocks it does not fit from the base profile: smear, stray light, pointing motion, hot pixels, CTI, layout and header style.

docs.title: Keyword map
docs.text: A keyword map names the header cards that hold each value. All entries are optional; with a time and a spacecraft state, refinement can match each real frame with a simulated twin. examples/keywords.json reads Skytwin's own keywords.

docs.title: Instrument profile reference
docs.text: Every key an instrument profile may hold. Every block is optional, and leaving one out switches that defect off. Use and override an instrument profile shows how a scene names a profile and changes it; design/realism.md explains the models.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
Wherever a defect block takes a number, it also takes a distribution; the numbers in the camera block are fixed. A defect setting such as pedestal_adu takes any of these forms:

"pedestal_adu": 24
"pedestal_adu": { "normal": [24, 8] }
"pedestal_adu": { "uniform": [12, 78] }
"pedestal_adu": { "log_uniform": [12, 78] }
"pedestal_adu": { "empirical": [12, 18, 24, 24, 31, 78] }

To keep settings that go together together, draw them from the same row:

"pedestal_adu":    { "empirical_linked": { "group": "real_frame", "values": [24, 31, 78] } },
"extra_white_adu": { "empirical_linked": { "group": "real_frame", "values": [26, 30, 43] } }

Every setting in one group takes the entry at the same index, so a frame that was measured warm and noisy stays warm and noisy. Lists in one group must have the same length.

A distribution is drawn once per frame from the frame's seed, in its own stream, so changing a profile setting does not change the pixel noise. Detector maps (hot pixels, bad columns, flat field) use a separate, fixed detector_seed, so they stay the same from frame to frame, as on a real chip.

docs.title: Profiles as contracts
docs.text:
A profile is one JSON file holding everything tuned to a sensor, so it can be handed to someone else and used as is. Learned profiles also say what they are and what they need:

Key Holds schema_version Profile format (1) sensor name, platform, band_nm [from, to], notes catalog The star catalogue the profile was calibrated against: name, kind (csv or ucac4), mag_limit, and for a CSV columns, epoch_jyear, sha256, rows; source says how to get or rebuild it learned Provenance: tool, version, commit, date, frames, inputs

The zeropoint, colour term and magnitude limit hold for that catalogue only. A scene that gives only the catalogue file gets the rest from the profile (anything the scene gives wins). A catalogue of the other kind is refused unless the scene sets "ignore_profile": true. Each run's provenance file records the catalogue used (with the CSV's SHA-256) beside the one the profile names.

docs.title: Profile layout
docs.text:
Every key below is optional. Units are in the key names.

Key Settings name, description Name (written to the truth file) and free text detector_seed Seed for everything fixed to the chip: column offsets, hot and flickering pixels, pixel response, dust (default 0) camera Image size, pixel scale and parity, PSF core, exposure, zeropoint, sky, gain, read noise, bias, full well, pixel pitch, distortion, colour term, passband sky_e_per_s Diffuse light per pixel, drawn per frame (replaces camera.sky; a zodiacal table still takes precedence) processing What the ground pipeline did: bias subtraction, pedestal, clipping, output type noise Extra white noise, coherent patterns, row and column offsets, ramps, serial lag, fixed and smooth fields temperature_c CCD temperature per frame dark Dark current at a reference temperature and how it scales with temperature hot_pixels, rts_pixels Hot pixels, and flickering (random telegraph) pixels, fixed to the chip radiation Hit rate, its map by sub-satellite position, charge per µm of track, charge spread cti Serial and parallel charge-transfer inefficiency readout_faults Rows lost or garbled in read-out psf Wings and a power-law tail beyond the core, and growth across the field flat Vignetting, pixel response non-uniformity, dust shadows, field stop smear, saturation Smear while charge moves; what happens above full well pointing Wobble, drift, jumps, oscillations and roll during the exposure, unresolved jitter, and the error of the header pointing stray_light, zodiacal Light from the Earth, Sun and Moon by angle; zodiacal light table detector Where the image sits on the chip: chip size, window, binning header FITS header written in the instrument's style sampling How finely moving sources are sampled schema_version, sensor, catalog, learned What a learned profile is and needs (see Profiles as contracts)

docs.title: processing
docs.text:
Key Meaning Default bias_subtracted The bias level was removed before delivery true pedestal_adu Offset added after processing 0 output Pixel type written: u16, i16, i32 or f32 u16 clip_min_adu, clip_max_adu Values outside are set to these the output type's range

u16 (0 to 65535) clips everything below 0, as many delivered products do. To keep the negative side of a bias-subtracted image, use i16, i32 or f32 and leave clip_min_adu unset. f32 also keeps fractional values; the integer types round.

docs.title: noise
docs.text:
Key Meaning extra_white_adu White Gaussian noise on top of the camera read noise, ADU RMS patterns Coherent plane waves A cos(2π(x cos θ + y sin θ)/P + φ), each with period_px, angle_deg, amplitude_adu; φ is random per frame row_noise_adu A new offset per row each frame, ADU RMS column_noise_adu An offset per column fixed to the detector (detector_seed), ADU RMS ramp_y_adu, ramp_y_adu_per_s Linear ramp from bottom to top: a fixed read-out part plus a part growing with exposure, ADU ramp_x_adu Linear ramp from left to right, ADU serial_lag Slow settling of the read-out chain: coefficient a (0 to below 1) and toward (left, the default, or right, the side trails extend to). See below fixed_field Additive structure that is the same every frame (a curved read-out ramp, glow near an edge, a bias pattern): values (ADU, rows of nodes), spacing_px, origin_px (pixel of node [0][0]); interpolated bilinearly, held at the edge value beyond the grid

sky_e_per_s (top level, any per-frame value) is diffuse light per pixel that replaces camera.sky: unlike processing.pedestal_adu it passes through the flat (vignetting, field stop) and carries shot noise.

docs.title: noise.serial_lag
docs.text: A single-pole low-pass along each row of the read-out signal, in read order: out = (1 − a) · in + a · previous out. It acts on charge and read noise alike, so it trails every source by aᵈ at d pixels and correlates the noise along rows (lag-k correlation aᵏ) but not down columns. CTI moves charge only and leaves the noise white; this is the analogue chain (a slow preamplifier or video filter). Flux is kept, and white noise variance falls by (1 − a)/(1 + a).

docs.title: temperature_c
docs.text: The CCD temperature, °C, drawn per frame. Scales dark and hot_pixels.

docs.title: dark
docs.text: Key Meaning e_per_s_at_ref Dark current at the reference temperature, e⁻/pixel/s (replaces camera.dark_e_per_s) ref_temp_c Reference temperature, °C doubling_c Optional: double every this many °C instead of following the silicon band-gap law

docs.title: hot_pixels
docs.text:
Key Meaning density_per_mpix Hot pixels per million pixels e_per_s_at_ref Each pixel's dark rate at the dark reference temperature, drawn once from detector_seed

The map is fixed to the detector; rates scale with the frame temperature like dark current.

docs.title: rts_pixels
docs.text:
Flickering pixels: dark current that switches at random between a low and a high level (random telegraph signal), common after radiation damage.

Key Meaning density_per_mpix Flickering pixels per million chip pixels (fixed by detector_seed) high_e_per_s_at_ref Extra rate in the high state at ref_temp_c, e⁻/s; scaled with temperature like dark current mean_high_s, mean_low_s Mean time in each state at ref_temp_c activation_high_ev, activation_low_ev Arrhenius activation energies of the switching: time constants shrink as the chip warms; different values change the fraction of time spent high

Each frame simulates the switching over the exposure. The truth file lists the pixels that were on and their mean rate.

docs.title: radiation
docs.text:
Key Meaning Default rate_per_cm2_s Hit rate when there is no map or no orbiting observer rate_map Rate table by sub-satellite latitude and longitude (lat_edges_deg, lon_edges_deg, rate_per_cm2_s rows) none map_scale Factor on the map, drawn per frame: an empirical distribution gives storms and belt edges, frames far above their cell's usual rate 1 collect_time_s Time hits accumulate the exposure readout_s Read-out time: each row keeps collecting hits until it is read, so hit density rises linearly to the last row read, which gets this much more time 0 first_row Row read first: bottom (row 0) or top bottom depth_um Sensitive silicon depth: sets track length from the incidence angle 15 e_per_um Most probable charge per µm of track 80 landau_scale Relative width of the charge straggling (Moyal) 0.15 diffusion_px Charge spread, Gaussian σ 0.4

The sub-satellite point needs scene.time and an orbiting scene.observer. State vectors may be Earth-fixed ("frame": "itrs"), as spacecraft headers often give them. The truth file lists every hit and the sub-satellite point.

docs.title: readout_faults
docs.text:
Rows lost or garbled after digitisation, as a link or memory fault leaves them.

Key Meaning Default probability Fraction of frames with any corruption bands Bands in a corrupted frame 1 band_rows Rows per band 1 kind_weights Relative weights of [noise, dropped, saturated]: salt and pepper (each pixel at the low clip or anywhere up to the high one), rows at the low clip, rows at the high clip [1, 1, 1] truncate_probability Chance that a corrupted frame is also cut short: every row from a random row to the last reads at the low clip 0 noise_low_fraction In a noise band, the share of pixels read at the low clip 0.5 noise_rms_adu In a noise band, the other pixels: unset, uniform over the whole output range (salt and pepper); set, the row's own value plus Gaussian noise of this RMS (drawn per band). With float output and no clip, garbled rows span the frame's own values unset

The truth file lists each band (readout_bands: first, last, kind).

docs.title: cti
docs.text: Key Meaning serial, parallel Each with loss_per_transfer and trail_px (mean release distance) amp_right, register_bottom Where charge is read out; trails point away from it

docs.title: noise.smooth_field
docs.text:
Smooth random background structure, new every frame: Gaussian values on a grid scale_px apart, interpolated with cubic B-splines, then set to zero mean and exactly rms_adu RMS over the frame. Real frames carry it from unresolved sources, scattered light and read-out drifts; without it, simulated backgrounds are too smooth.

Key Meaning rms_adu RMS over the frame, ADU scale_px Grid spacing (feature size), pixels

docs.title: camera
docs.text:
The numbers in camera are fixed; they don't take a distribution.

Key Meaning Default width, height Image size, pixels 1024, 1024 pixel_scale_arcsec Pixel scale, arcsec per pixel 3.0 parity Handedness on the sky: negative (north up, east left) or positive (mirrored) negative optical_axis_px Pixel [x, y] (0-based) on the optical axis, where the pointing is image centre distortion Radial distortion about the optical axis: k1, k2 (coefficients of ρ² and ρ⁴, ρ in units of radius_px), radius_px; negative k1 is barrel none (pure TAN) fwhm_px PSF core full width at half maximum, pixels 2.5 exposure_s Exposure time, s; 0 makes a bias frame, which can hold no stars, streaks or targets 10.0 zeropoint_mag Magnitude giving 1 e⁻/s in total, all losses folded in 20.0 sky Sky background: {"e_per_s": …} per pixel or {"mag_per_arcsec2": …} {"mag_per_arcsec2": 22.5} dark_e_per_s Dark current, e⁻ per pixel per second (replaced by dark) 0.1 read_noise_e Read noise, e⁻ RMS 8.0 gain_e_per_adu Gain, e⁻ per ADU 1.5 bias_adu Bias level, ADU 1000.0 full_well_e Full well, e⁻; pixels clip here before digitising 60,000 pixel_pitch_um Pixel pitch, µm; sets the area radiation hits fall on 13.0 quantum_efficiency Electrons per incident photon, for photon counts in the truth; the zeropoint stays in electrons 1.0 sun_mag The Sun's magnitude in the camera band, for light reflected by targets −26.74 (V) earth_limb_margin_km Height above the surface below which a line of sight counts as blocked, km 100 color_term Catalogue-to-camera colour term (below) none passband Passband and collecting area (below); replaces zeropoint_mag and sun_mag none

docs.title: camera.color_term
docs.text: Moves catalogue magnitudes to the camera band: m_camera = m_catalogue + coefficient × colour index. bands names the two catalogue bands of the index (first minus second, for example ["apass_b", "apass_v"]); catalogue stars get their index from those bands, and default_index serves stars without both. Without bands, stars take the catalogue's own colour column (a CSV catalogue's bp_rp). Scene stars may give color_index. The truth file records each star's index.

docs.title: camera.passband
docs.text:
A passband replaces camera.zeropoint_mag and camera.sun_mag with values computed by synthetic photometry in AB magnitudes:

Key Meaning name Written as FILTER response wavelength_nm and throughput (0–1): optics × filter × quantum efficiency aperture_area_m2 Collecting area reference Optional curve of the band magnitudes are given in, such as the catalogue's; stars move to the camera band by their temperature color_index b_v or bp_rp: what a star's color_index is, to get its temperature color_bands UCAC4 bands of that index (first minus second) default_teff_k Temperature for stars without one (default 5800 K)

The zeropoint is the AB magnitude giving 1 e⁻/s, 2.5 log10(A/h ∫ 3631 Jy T(λ) dλ/λ). Sources are blackbodies: stars at their temperature (scene teff_k, else from the colour index, else the default), the Sun at 5772 K and 1 au, so reflected light from targets follows the band. A star's camera magnitude is its reference magnitude plus the difference of the two bands' AB magnitudes for its blackbody, tabulated over 2000–50,000 K. Give either color_term or reference, not both. The header adds MAGSYS = 'AB'; MAGZERO is the computed zeropoint.

docs.title: psf
docs.text:
Key Meaning wings Wider Gaussian components, each with fraction (share of the flux) and fwhm_px; the core (camera.fwhm_px) keeps the rest tail A power-law (Moffat) tail: fraction, fwhm_px, beta (wings fall as r^−2β, β > 1); expanded into ten Gaussians fitted to the profile out to 12 FWHM field.radial_growth, field.tangential_growth Fractional growth of every component's σ along and across the radius from the optical axis, reached at the image's half-diagonal (quadratic in radius, like coma and astigmatism)

Every component is pixel-integrated and applies to stars, trails, streaks and targets alike. A field-dependent PSF is an elliptical Gaussian.

docs.title: flat
docs.text:
Key Meaning vignetting [a2, a4]: response 1 + a2 ρ² + a4 ρ⁴, ρ the distance from the optical axis in half-diagonals prnu_rms Pixel response non-uniformity, fractional RMS, fixed to each chip pixel dust Out-of-focus dust shadows (annular "donuts") fixed to the chip: density_per_mpix, radius_px, depth (fraction of light removed), hole_fraction (inner radius over outer) field_stop A circular aperture imaged on the chip: radius_px (half response), edge_px (Gaussian σ of the edge), outside (response beyond, as a fraction of inside), centre_px (default: the optical axis). Response outside + (1 − outside) · ½ erfc((r − radius) / (√2 edge))

The flat multiplies light only. skytwin … --write-flat also writes the noiseless flat as name.flat.fits (32-bit floats), for testing flat-fielding. The truth file lists the dust shadows. With hole_fraction 0 the shadows are solid dark blobs, as dust closer to focus casts.

docs.title: smear
docs.text:
Key Meaning above_s_per_row Seconds each row's charge spends under a source while moving, for pixels above it (higher row numbers) below_s_per_row The same for pixels below it

Without a shutter, light keeps falling while charge is flushed before the exposure and transferred after it. A source of rate R e⁻/s then adds R × dwell to every pixel of its column, on each side. Only light smears: dark current and hot pixels are added afterwards.

docs.title: saturation
docs.text:
Key Meaning Default bleed Charge above camera.full_well_e spills along the column, half each way, conserving charge false (excess lost) serial_overflow A share of the excess spills along the row first, as when the serial register overflows, drawing a horizontal line from a saturated star: fraction of the excess, exponential length_px, toward left (default) or right none

If the ADC saturates before the pixel's full well, as on some cameras, set processing.clip_max_adu to the ADC limit and leave bleed off.

docs.title: pointing
docs.text:
Motion of the whole image during the exposure, and the error of the pointing written to the header.

Key Meaning wobble_rms_arcsec, wobble_time_s Smooth random wander per axis (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck), RMS and correlation time (default 1 s) drift_arcsec_per_s Steady rate in a random direction, zero at mid-exposure drift_turn_deg_per_s Rate at which the drift direction turns, in a random sense: the image moves along a circular arc of radius rate / turn rate, and every star trails in the same arc roll_rate_deg_per_s, roll_centre_px Rotation of the image about a pixel (default: the image centre), in a random sense, zero at mid-exposure: stars trail in arcs centred there, longer the farther they are from it jump_rate_per_s, jump_arcsec Sudden offsets at random times, random directions blur_arcsec Unresolved fast jitter: a Gaussian σ added to every PSF component oscillations Sinusoids, each amplitude_arcsec, period_s and angle_deg on the image (default random per frame), random phase. The image dwells at the turning points: along a trail they draw dashes, across it a zigzag or, when fast, two parallel trails header.reference_px Pixel whose sky position the reported RA/Dec describe (default: image centre) header.error_arcsec, header.roll_error_deg Random error of the reported pointing (σ per axis) and roll header.epoch When the reported pointing applies: start, mid (default) or end of the exposure

Motion moves stars, targets and streaks; it does not move radiation hits or hot pixels, which belong to the detector. The path is measured from the image at mid-exposure: whatever wobble, oscillation or jumps came before, the image is then where it would be without motion, so the star positions in the truth and the header WCS describe that moment. Trail ends, streak ends and target samples in the truth are where each source was drawn, motion included. The truth file keeps the offset path (thinned), every jump, and the turn and roll rates. The header's ATT_RA, ATT_DEC, ATT_ROLL carry the reported pointing; the truth file keeps both the true and the reported pointing.

camera.parity (negative, the default, or positive) mirrors the image for optics that flip it; roll stays the position angle of +y.

camera.distortion adds radial lens distortion about the optical axis: a point the TAN projection puts r pixels from the axis lands at r (1 + k1 ρ² + k2 ρ⁴), ρ = r / radius_px (k1 negative: barrel; positive: pincushion). Every star, target, streak and truth position goes through it, and the header WCS becomes TAN-SIP with order-5 A/B and AP/BP terms fitted to the model over the disc of radius_px (use the half-diagonal so the whole frame is covered).

docs.title: stray_light
docs.text:
A list, one entry per body. Needs scene.time, an orbiting scene.observer and a pointing.

Key Meaning body earth (angle to the nearest limb), sun or moon (angle to the centre) angle_deg, e_per_s Level at the image centre against angle, e⁻/pixel/s; log-interpolated, held below the table, zero beyond it gradient How much brighter the bright edge is than the centre, across half the frame width (0.2 = 20%) toward_deg Direction of the bright side relative to the body's direction in the image: 0 towards it, 180 away from it dark_limb_factor Earth: factor when the nearest limb point is in darkness phase_scaled Moon: scale by the illuminated fraction (default true)

The truth file records each source's angle, level, image direction and whether the limb was lit (Moon: lit fraction).

docs.title: zodiacal
docs.text: A table of zodiacal surface brightness, V mag/arcsec², with elongation_deg (|λ − λ☉|), latitude_deg (|β|) and v_mag_arcsec2 rows by elongation. With a time and an observer it replaces camera.sky; the V value is moved to the camera band through camera.sun_mag, since zodiacal light has the Sun's colour. Skytwin ships no table: fill it from a published reference such as Leinert et al. (1998), table 17.

docs.title: sampling
docs.text:
How finely moving sources (streaks, trails, targets) are cut into exact straight pieces.

Key Meaning Default pixel_tolerance Largest distance between the true path and a piece, px 0.01 flux_relative_tolerance Largest relative brightness error over a piece 0.01 max_step_s Longest piece, s none max_depth Deepest halving of a piece 14

docs.title: detector
docs.text:
Where the delivered image sits on the chip.

Key Meaning Default chip_px Chip size, unbinned pixels the image size window_origin_px Chip pixel of the image's first pixel, unbinned, 0-based [0, 0] binning Binning [x, y] [1, 1]

camera describes the delivered image (its size, pixel scale and PSF are in binned pixels). The layout moves the chip's own effects into place: hot pixels belong to the chip, so two windows of one chip share them (binned pixels sum theirs); radiation hits see the binned pixel area and track length; CTI counts transfers from the window's real distance to the amplifier and register. camera.optical_axis_px puts the pointing on a given image pixel instead of the centre.

docs.title: header
docs.text:
Key Meaning Default wcs Write the WCS true skytwin_keywords Write Skytwin's own keywords (times, observer, attitude, seed) true roll keyword, offset_deg, sign: the roll in the instrument's convention, offset + sign × roll none cards Extra cards in order: key, value, comment none sexagesimal_carry Carry rounded seconds into the minutes. false copies a common formatter bug: 59.96 s is written 60.0, about one frame in 600 per field true wrong_wcs Write a wrong WCS on some frames, as another solver's failed solution: probability, offset_arcmin (tangent point moved, random direction), roll_deg (axes turned, either way), scale_error none

A card value is a number, a boolean, a string, or a template computed from the frame: {date_obs}, {jd_obs}, {mjd_obs}, {exposure_s}, {ccd_temp_c}, {ccd_temp_k}, {ra_deg}, {dec_deg}, {roll_deg}, {ra_hms}, {dec_dms} (option :space for hh mm ss.s), {sub_lat_deg}, {sub_lon_deg}, {earth_limb_deg}, {binning_x}, {binning_y}. Option :str writes a number as a quoted string. A template whose value the frame lacks (no time, no observer) is left out. A card named like one of Skytwin's own keywords replaces it.

With wrong_wcs, the truth file keeps the true wcs and adds the header_wcs that was written instead. A scene's header_bias_arcsec ([east, north]) shifts the reported RA/Dec from the true pointing, on top of pointing.header.error_arcsec: a header that lags the boresight.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: The skytwin package renders frames in memory and turns their truth into labels. The export guide shows the package in use; this page lists every public name, from the package's docstrings.

docs.title: skytwin
docs.text:
Skytwin from Python: simulated frames and exact labels, in memory.

import skytwin
sim = skytwin.Simulator("scene.json")      # a scene file, or a dict
for frame in sim.stream(count=1000):        # rendered ahead on all cores
    frame.image                             # numpy array (rows, columns)
    frame.truth["stars"], frame.truth["streaks"]

Frame k uses seed + k and draws everything random anew; with batch.random_pointing it also points somewhere new. A frame depends only on its index, so the same index always gives the same pixels, whatever the order or the number of workers.

docs.title: Simulator
docs.text:
A scene file loaded once, to render many frames.

scene is a path to a scene file or the same content as a dict. Instrument profile paths inside it are read relative to the working directory. seed replaces the file's seed.

docs.title: render(index=0, *, expected=False)
docs.text: Render frame index (thread-safe; the GIL is released).

docs.title: stream(start=0, count=None, *, workers=None, prefetch=None, expected=False)
docs.text: Frames start to start + count - 1 in order, rendered ahead on workers threads (default: every core), at most prefetch finished frames waiting (default: 2 per worker). count defaults to the rest of the batch.

docs.title: Frame
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

One simulated frame.

docs.title: index instance-attribute
docs.text: Index in the batch.

docs.title: seed instance-attribute
docs.text: Seed it was drawn with (the file's seed + index).

docs.title: image instance-attribute
docs.text: Pixels as delivered (the profile's output type), shape (rows, columns).

docs.title: truth instance-attribute
docs.text: Everything drawn: stars, streaks, targets, WCS, pointing, detector effects (the same as the .truth.json file).

docs.title: expected instance-attribute
docs.text: Noise-free electrons per pixel (float32), when asked for: a clean target for denoising or detection.

docs.title: skytwin.labels
docs.text:
Detector labels from a frame's truth: boxes, rotated boxes, YOLO and COCO.

Every star, streak and target in the truth carries a label: the path it was drawn along, the signal-to-noise of an ideal matched filter, the peak pixel signal-to-noise, how far from the path it stands above the pixel noise, and whether it saturates. :func:objects turns those into labelled objects; :func:boxes cuts them to a tile of the image (or the whole of it) as axis-aligned and rotated boxes; :func:yolo_lines, :func:yolo_obb_lines and :func:coco_annotations write them out.

Coordinates. Skytwin puts pixel centres on whole numbers: (0, 0) is the centre of image[0, 0]. YOLO and COCO measure from the outer corner of that pixel, so every label here is shifted by half a pixel. x runs along a row and y down the array; images are written with array row 0 at the top, so a FITS viewer that draws row 0 at the bottom shows the same frame flipped vertically.

Classes. Stars are star; targets and pixel streaks are satellite. With by_form each splits into _point and _streak by how far apart the farthest two points of its drawn path are: a streak spans more than twice the PSF FWHM. Pointing jitter and small jumps leave a source a point; tracking at a target's rate trails every star into a streak and keeps the target a point.

docs.title: CLASSES = ('star', 'satellite') module-attribute
docs.text: Class names, in YOLO order.

docs.title: FORM_CLASSES = ('star_point', 'star_streak', 'satellite_point', 'satellite_streak') module-attribute
docs.text: Class names when split by form, in YOLO order.

docs.title: Obj dataclass
docs.text: One labelled source, in Skytwin pixel coordinates.

docs.title: kind instance-attribute
docs.text: star or satellite.

docs.title: form instance-attribute
docs.text: point or streak.

docs.title: path instance-attribute
docs.text: Drawn path, shape (n, 2), [x, y] with pixel centres on whole numbers.

docs.title: radius instance-attribute
docs.text: Half-width of the labelled region about the path, px (to pixel edges).

docs.title: snr instance-attribute
docs.text: Matched-filter signal-to-noise over the whole image.

docs.title: peak_snr instance-attribute
docs.text: Highest single-pixel signal-to-noise.

docs.title: saturated instance-attribute
docs.text: Whether it reaches full well.

docs.title: source instance-attribute
docs.text: Where it is in the truth: stars[3], streaks[0] or targets[0].

docs.title: name property
docs.text: Class name with the form: star_point, satellite_streak, …

docs.title: Box dataclass
docs.text: An object cut to a tile, in that tile's corner coordinates (pixels).

docs.title: xyxy instance-attribute
docs.text: Axis-aligned box (x0, y0, x1, y1).

docs.title: corners instance-attribute
docs.text: Rotated box: four corners in order around it, inside the tile. A streak's box is a rectangle along it, cut by the tile's edge where it crosses one (see boxes).

docs.title: snr instance-attribute
docs.text: Matched-filter signal-to-noise of the part inside the tile (for a streak, the whole value scaled by the square root of the share of its on-image length inside).

docs.title: class_names(by_form=False, kinds=CLASSES)
docs.text: Class names in YOLO order for the chosen kinds.

docs.title: objects(truth, *, min_radius_px=None, streak_px=None)
docs.text:
Every source in a frame's truth that has a drawn path.

radius is the label's extent_px or min_radius_px (default: the camera FWHM), whichever is larger, plus half a pixel to reach the edges of the outermost pixels. A source is a streak when the farthest two points of its path are more than streak_px apart (default: twice the FWHM), and otherwise a point.

docs.title: boxes(objs, tile, image_size, *, min_snr=5.0, min_visible=0.5)
docs.text:
Objects cut to tile = (x0, y0, width, height) in pixels of an image of image_size = (width, height).

A point is kept when at least min_visible of its box area lies in the tile; a streak when part of its path does. Either needs a signal-to-noise of at least min_snr inside the tile. A point's box is its path widened by its radius; a streak's is the part of its path within a radius of the tile, widened by the radius; both are clamped to the tile. A streak's rotated box runs along its part in the tile from the first to the last point, cut by the tile's edge where it crosses one, so it holds all of the streak inside the tile; a point's is its box.

docs.title: class_id(o, names)
docs.text: Index of an object's class in names (with or without its form), or None.

docs.title: yolo_lines(bxs, names, tile_size)
docs.text: Ultralytics detection labels: class cx cy w h, normalised.

docs.title: yolo_obb_lines(bxs, names, tile_size)
docs.text: Ultralytics oriented-box labels: class x1 y1 x2 y2 x3 y3 x4 y4, normalised.

docs.title: coco_annotations(bxs, names, image_id, first_id)
docs.text: COCO annotations (bbox as [x, y, w, h], category ids from 1), each with a skytwin record: form, signal-to-noise, saturation, rotated box and source in the truth.

docs.title: tiles(width, height, size=None, overlap=0)
docs.text: Tiles (x0, y0, w, h) of at most size px covering the image, overlapping by at least overlap px, the last in each row and column flush with the edge. One tile (the image) without a size.

docs.title: stretch(image, *, soft=3.0, top=1000.0)
docs.text:
8-bit image for a detector: noise-normalised, then an asinh stretch.

The image is measured in units of its noise, z = (image − median) / σ with σ from the median absolute deviation, and z from −2 to top maps through asinh(z / soft) onto 0–255. A source's grey level then depends on its signal-to-noise alone, the same in every frame however bright the sky.

docs.title: raw16(image)
docs.text: The image as delivered, as 16-bit unsigned (other types rounded and clipped).

docs.title: write_png(path, image, level=3)
docs.text: Write a 2-D uint8 or uint16 array as a greyscale PNG, row 0 at the top.

docs.title: skytwin.torch
docs.text:
A PyTorch dataset of simulated frames, rendered on the fly.

from skytwin.torch import FrameDataset, collate, detection_target
ds = FrameDataset("scene.json", transform=detection_target)
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(ds, batch_size=16, num_workers=4, collate_fn=collate)
for images, targets in loader:
    ...                                        # targets[i]["boxes"], targets[i]["labels"]

Each DataLoader worker renders its own share of the indices, on threads Rust threads. transform(frame) turns a :class:skytwin.Frame into whatever the model takes; by default it gives the image as a float32 tensor and the frame's index, which PyTorch's default collation batches. :func:detection_target gives the stretched image and boxes in the form torchvision detectors (xyxy) or DETR (cxcywh) take. Frames hold different numbers of objects, so batch them with :func:collate, which stacks the images and keeps one target per image; PyTorch's default collation cannot.

docs.title: FrameDataset
docs.text:
Bases: IterableDataset

Frames start to start + count - 1 of a scene file's batch.

Under a DataLoader each worker renders one contiguous share of the indices, on threads Rust threads (default 1 per worker; every core without workers).

docs.title: default_transform(frame)
docs.text:
The image as a float32 tensor, and the frame's index.

The index, not the truth dict, so a plain DataLoader can batch the pairs; frames hold different numbers of objects, which PyTorch's default collation cannot stack. For labels, use :func:detection_target with :func:collate.

docs.title: detection_target(frame, *, kinds=lab.CLASSES, by_form=False, streak_px=None, min_snr=5.0, box_format='xyxy')
docs.text:
The frame as a detector's input and target.

The image is :func:skytwin.labels.stretch scaled to 0–1, shape (1, rows, columns). The target holds boxes (xyxy in pixels from the image corner, or cxcywh as fractions of the image), class indices labels into :func:skytwin.labels.class_names, each object's snr, and the frame's index.

docs.title: collate(batch)
docs.text: Stack the images of (image, target) pairs and keep the targets as a list.

docs.title: skytwin.export
docs.text:
Write a training set: images with YOLO, YOLO-OBB or COCO labels.

skytwin-export scene.json out/ --frames 5000 --format yolo --format coco --tile 640

Layout, as Ultralytics and COCO tools expect it::

out/images/{train,val}/000123.png              000123_04.png for tile 4
out/labels/{train,val}/000123.txt              YOLO or YOLO-OBB
out/data.yaml                                  Ultralytics dataset file
out/annotations/instances_{train,val}.json     COCO; file names relative to images/<split>/
out/skytwin.json                               what was rendered, with which options

Frame k is the scene's frame k (seed + k), so the set can be rebuilt or extended exactly. The last --val share of the frames (rounded up) is the validation split, and every tile of a frame stays in its frame's split. Images are the delivered pixels through :func:skytwin.labels.stretch (8-bit, noise-normalised asinh) or, with --image raw16, as delivered in 16 bits. Labels are those of :mod:skytwin.labels: objects at or above --min-snr (matched-filter signal-to-noise) inside each tile.

docs.title: Your first training set¶
docs.text: In this tutorial you describe a camera with a few real-world defects, render a frame through it, look at the labels Skytwin gives every star and satellite streak, and export 200 frames as a YOLO training set. It takes about five minutes and needs no data of your own: every frame is made here.

docs.title: Describe the camera¶
docs.text:
A scene renders through an instrument profile. Here the profile is written inline: a 512 × 512 camera with 3″ pixels, plus three defects that real frames carry and clean simulations usually lack. Hot pixels and radiation hits look like faint stars to a detector; the pattern noise is a faint diagonal ripple. Values written as uniform or log_uniform are drawn anew for each frame, so the set spreads the way a real archive does.

The scene scatters 300 stars and one to three satellite streaks over the field.

docs.title: Render a frame¶
docs.text: Simulator loads the scene once; render(k) gives frame k, drawn with seed + k. The image comes back as the camera would deliver it, and the truth holds everything that was drawn.

docs.title: Read the labels¶
docs.text: Every star and streak in the truth carries a label: the path it was drawn along and its matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio against this frame's noise. labels.objects turns them into objects with a class and a form. A source is labelled for training when its ratio reaches 5, so faint stars a detector cannot find are not counted against it.

docs.title: Export a training set¶
docs.text: skytwin-export renders frames 0 to 199 of the same scene on every core and writes them as PNG tiles with YOLO label files. The scene goes in a JSON file first. The last 10% of the frames become the validation split.

docs.title: What you built¶
docs.text:
first-set/ is a YOLO dataset of 800 tiles from 200 frames of a camera with hot pixels, radiation hits and pattern noise, with every star and streak above signal-to-noise 5 labelled. Ultralytics reads it as is:

pip install ultralytics
yolo detect train data=first-set/data.yaml model=yolo11n.pt imgsz=256

To go further:

  • Export a training set covers COCO output, rotated boxes and loading frames straight into PyTorch.
  • Use and override an instrument profile renders through the profiles learned from real cameras.
  • The labels reference lists every option and file.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Skytwin is developed and maintained by Shane Ryall.

Skytwin is a simulator, written in Rust with Python bindings, of what a camera sees when it looks for satellites and other resident space objects, from orbit or from the ground. A frame from a real camera comes with no list of what is in it. A frame from Skytwin comes with a truth file that gives the position, path, flux and signal-to-noise ratio of every star, streak and target. That makes it a test bench for detectors, trackers and plate solvers (such as Fayde), and a source of labelled training data for space domain awareness.

Stars are placed by hand, at random, or read from UCAC4 or a Gaia extract and moved to the observation epoch; with a sky pointing, the FITS header carries a TAN or TAN-SIP WCS. Observers and targets come from TLEs, state vectors or ephemeris tables, with light-time, Earth shadow, glints from tumbling facets, and refraction and extinction for a ground site. An instrument profile holds every detector and optics defect as a setting, fixed or drawn per frame. The same scene file and seed give the same pixels on every machine.

The pictures in this file are synthetic frames made by scripts/make_readme_figures.py. Each frame is shown with the asinh stretch that skytwin-export writes, so its grey levels follow its own noise and can't be compared across frames. The first picture shows random stars through each shipped instrument profile, a 164-pixel crop from the centre of each frame at the camera's own pixel scale:

docs.title: Skytwin
docs.text:
Synthetic star-field images with satellite streaks, instrument defects and an exact answer key for every frame.

Install · Quick start · Tutorial · Profiles · Labels · Documentation · Changelog

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The command needs Rust 1.85 or later. To install it from a checkout:

cargo install --path crates/skytwin-cli

The Python package, which also provides the skytwin-export command, and skytwin-calibrate need Python 3.10 or later. In a virtual environment, from the repository root:

pip install ./crates/skytwin-py

pip install -e tools/calibrate

A star catalogue, a UCAC4 directory or a Gaia CSV extract, is optional; scenes need one only for real skies.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Render the example scene from the repository root:

cargo run --release -p skytwin-cli -- examples/two-streaks.json out/two-streaks.fits

This writes out/two-streaks.fits, its answer key out/two-streaks.truth.json, and out/two-streaks.provenance.json. In the truth file, streaks[0] gives the first streak's start and end pixels and its flux_e. --seed N overrides the scene's seed.

More scenes, from a camera in a 790 km orbit to a ground telescope tracking a MEO satellite, are in examples/. Four of them, leo-observer, leo-stares-geo, leo-tracks-geo, and ucac4-field, read their stars from a UCAC4 catalogue at data/ucac4. To render them, copy UCAC4 to data/ucac4, or set scene.catalog.ucac4 in the scene file to the path of your copy. examples/tumbling-glint.json renders a tumbling target whose panels reflect the Sun towards the camera once in the exposure. The truth file records the signal along its streak:

Each pixel draws its noise from its own random stream, so the same seed with and without a satellite gives an exact clean and dirty pair. In the next picture, made with the example profile without its frame-transfer smear, the two whole 1024 × 1024 frames differ in 4,565 pixels, all where the streak's light falls; the difference panel is on a linear scale:

docs.title: Training sets
docs.text:
The --frames option renders independent frames on all cores, and frame k uses the scene's seed plus k. To render 20 frames of examples/dirty-frame.json from the repository root:

skytwin examples/dirty-frame.json out/batch/f.fits --frames 20 --compact-truth

Each frame of this scene is a 2 MB FITS file, so a set of 50,000 frames takes about 105 GB.

From Python, frames arrive as numpy arrays with their truth, with exactly the pixels of the same frame from --frames:

import skytwin

sim = skytwin.Simulator("examples/dirty-frame.json")
for frame in sim.stream(count=20):
    image, stars = frame.image, frame.truth["stars"]

To write a set that Ultralytics YOLO and COCO tools such as DETR read directly:

skytwin-export examples/dirty-frame.json out/yolo/ --frames 20 --format yolo --format coco --tile 640

Stars are class star, and targets and streaks are class satellite. An object is labelled when its matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio in the tile reaches 5, the default. The next picture draws the rotated boxes that --format yolo-obb writes, blue for stars and orange for satellites. --format yolo writes axis-aligned boxes around the same objects, and COCO records both:

docs.title: Instrument profiles
docs.text:
A profile is one JSON file holding everything tuned to a sensor: noise, pattern noise, dark current, hot and flickering pixels, radiation hits, charge-transfer trails, smear, saturation, flat field, stray light, pointing motion and the FITS header style. The next picture turns on one defect at a time in a plain camera, with settings strong enough to see:

To learn a profile from sample frames, with the installed skytwin refining it, and print what it holds:

skytwin-calibrate learn FRAMES_DIR -o profile.json --skytwin skytwin --catalog GAIA_CSV

skytwin-calibrate describe profile.json

FRAMES_DIR is a folder of FITS frames and GAIA_CSV a Gaia extract. profiles/cassiope-fai-nir.json was learned this way from the public DUST dataset, frames of the CASSIOPE Fast Auroral Imager's near-infrared channel.
